strengths: The core idea—detecting 3D Gaussian primitives at sub-pixel 2D locations via heatmap soft-argmax instead of using a rigid pixel/voxel grid—is simple, intuitive, and well motivated. It transfers keypoint detection ideas to feed-forward 3DGS in a sensible way.

The adaptive density allocation based on patch entropy and the learned per-primitive confidence for multi-view aggregation are supported by the ablation in Table 3: detection + adaptive density + confidence reaches the best PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS among the ablated variants.

Table 1 provides strong empirical evidence on DL3DV and Charge: the method achieves state-of-the-art novel-view synthesis among pose-free feed-forward methods across sparse-view settings while using far fewer Gaussians (e.g., 115.2k vs 314.8k on 3-view DL3DV; 460.4k vs 2152.7k on 12-view DL3DV).

Table 2 and the supplementary focal-length tables show that self-supervised rendering-based fine-tuning improves camera pose estimation over both VGGT and AnySplat, which is a useful and somewhat surprising result for 3D foundation models.

The paper is clearly written, with a well-illustrated architecture and training pipeline. The self-supervised training setup, losses, and implementation choices are described in enough detail to support reproducibility, with additional supplementary material.
The approach is pose-free and requires no 3D annotations, making it practical for scaling feed-forward 3DGS and potentially useful for improving geometry backbones through rendering supervision.
weaknesses: The evaluation is somewhat narrow: only DL3DV and Charge are used, and the main comparison omits other pose-free feed-forward 3DGS methods cited in related work, such as NoPoSplat, Splatt3R, and SPFSplat. The claim of state-of-the-art feed-forward NVS is therefore not comprehensively established.

The efficiency claim is only partially supported. The paper reports Gaussian counts but no quantitative runtime, memory, or FPS measurements, even though the abstract and introduction emphasize real-time/second-scale generation and fewer primitives as a central benefit.

Depth estimation results are mixed rather than clearly improved. On Charge, the method is worse than VGGT on AbsRel and/or δ<1.25 in several view settings (e.g., 3 views: AbsRel 0.1189 vs 0.1039; 9 views: AbsRel 0.1048 vs 0.0992). The claim that the method improves 3D geometry is therefore strongest for camera pose and qualitative depth, not uniformly for quantitative depth.

The method depends heavily on the VGGT backbone, and no experiments test the decoder with another reconstruction backbone or without VGGT. This makes it difficult to judge how much of the gain comes from the proposed primitive detection versus the pretrained backbone and its fine-tuning.

Several hyperparameters appear heuristic—entropy thresholds 55/35/15, heatmap softmax temperature 0.2, and confidence pruning threshold 0.1—and no sensitivity analysis is provided. The multi-view aggregation also risks duplicate or collapsed primitives within patches, which is not analyzed.

The test-time alignment protocol follows AnySplat and may affect baseline comparisons; the poor FLARE results are partly attributed to protocol issues, but this also raises questions about the fairness and generality of the reported ranking.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated formulation: casting Gaussian primitive placement as a detection problem with continuous sub-pixel 2D coordinates (soft-argmax / DSNT over heatmaps) rather than a rigid pixel- or voxel-aligned grid. This is a clean departure from prior feed-forward 3DGS decoders and is convincingly justified in the introduction and related work.

Strong efficiency story backed by numbers: Table 1 shows state-of-the-art PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS on DL3DV and Charge while using roughly 7x fewer primitives than pixel-aligned competitors (e.g., 115.2K vs 314.8K at 3 views), and the ablation in Table 3 (19.09 PSNR / 38,400 Gaussians vs 19.02 / 268,324 for the pixel-aligned baseline) directly supports the claim that a dense regular grid is unnecessary.

Two additional mechanisms are principled and ablated: entropy-based adaptive density allocation (APT) and a learned per-Gaussian confidence used for multi-view aggregation and test-time pruning. Figure 5 gives a nice qualitative demonstration that the confidence implicitly performs multi-view reasoning and discards redundantly observed primitives.

Interesting and potentially impactful secondary finding: self-supervised fine-tuning through rendering supervision improves the VGGT backbone's camera pose estimation (Table 2, AUC@15 0.7887 vs 0.7599 at 3 views), suggesting a route to label-free refinement of 3D foundation models.

Evaluation is reasonably thorough for a conference paper: two datasets, four view-count regimes (3/6/9/12 and dense 25), quantitative ablations, plus supplementary depth and focal-length analyses with clear failure-case discussion.
Reproducibility is good: implementation details (backbone, UNet channels, softmax temperature, grid_sample padding, training data and sampling) are provided in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: Novelty of the core building blocks is incremental: soft-argmax/DSNT sub-pixel keypoint regression, entropy-based adaptive token/patch allocation, and confidence-based pruning are all existing techniques; the contribution is their (sensible) repurposing for 3DGS decoding. The paper would benefit from more clearly positioning this against those prior uses.

Geometry-related claims are overstated relative to the evidence. On Charge, depth is actually worse than VGGT (AbsRel 0.1189 vs 0.1039; delta<1.25 0.8395 vs 0.8669) and focal-length FoV error is worse (2.07 vs 1.69 in Table 4). The narrative of 'improved geometry' is only partially supported and should be qualified per metric/dataset.

At matched resolution the detection-vs-pixel-aligned gain is small (19.09 vs 19.02 PSNR in Table 3), so a large share of the headline advantage comes from efficiency rather than fidelity; the abstract could be more precise about this trade-off.

Baseline concerns: FLARE fails at test-time alignment (the authors note this has been reported before, but it still weakens that comparison), VGGT+DepthSplat is an ad-hoc combination of a pose-required method with a pose-free backbone, and the pixel-aligned and voxel-aligned baselines are internal reimplementations. It is unclear how much of the reported margin reflects the best possible configuration of prior art.

The method only reconstructs visible areas and leaves holes for regions missed during capture (acknowledged in Sec. 5), which limits applicability and is not quantified (e.g., no hole/completeness metric).

Some reporting details are ambiguous: the semantics of the reported Gaussian counts (training vs post-pruning, per-scene vs aggregated) and the exact test-time alignment protocol are not fully transparent in the main text, making it harder to assess the efficiency comparisons at face value.

The pose-estimation improvements, while real on DL3DV, are modest and inconsistent across datasets, and the paper does not isolate how much of this comes from the detection decoder versus the additional teacher-geometry losses.

strengths: Proposes a detection-based decoder that places Gaussian primitives at continuous sub-pixel 2D locations, avoiding rigid pixel/voxel grid assignment.
Adaptive density via patch entropy and learned confidence for multi-view aggregation/pruning are sensible and supported by ablation.
Strong results on DL3DV: outperforms AnySplat, FLARE, and VGGT+DepthSplat in PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS across view counts with far fewer primitives (e.g., 115.2k vs 314.8k/344.1k at 3 views).
Demonstrates that fine-tuning VGGT with rendering supervision improves camera pose AUC on Charge over VGGT and AnySplat, suggesting self-improvement of 3D foundation models.
Honest limitations section and some failure analysis, e.g., holes in unseen regions and depth degradation on far backgrounds.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to two datasets and inconsistent: on Charge sparse settings (3 and 6 views), PSNR/SSIM are lower than VGGT+DepthSplat (e.g., 17.38 vs 19.37 PSNR at 3 views), so the 'state-of-the-art' claim is not uniformly supported.
Missing comparisons to other relevant pose-free feed-forward methods such as NoPoSplat, Splatt3R, and PF3Splat, which are cited but not quantitatively evaluated.

Method is incremental: it combines existing ideas (keypoint detection via DSNT/soft-argmax, adaptive density inspired by APT, confidence-based pruning) without a fundamentally new formulation; 'off-the-grid' is only within patches, not globally grid-free.

Technical inconsistencies and missing details: density percentages 55%+35%+15%=105%; L_op is written as sin(α·c) (likely a sigmoid typo); no explicit confidence supervision; hard density assignment may cause patch-boundary artifacts.

The 'self-supervised/without annotation' claim is overstated: training uses VGGT teacher geometry losses and a VGGT backbone pretrained on large annotated 3D data; the teacher regularizes toward VGGT, potentially limiting improvements.

Reproducibility concerns: no code release; unusual 'single GPU with 140 GB of VRAM'; missing training hyperparameters, runtime, memory, and inference time; project page link is absent in the manuscript.

Depth estimation metrics are worse than VGGT across all view counts in Table 2 (AbsRel and δ<1.25), while qualitative improvement is claimed only in supplementary material without quantitative support.

Ablation gains over pixel-aligned baselines are modest (PSNR 19.09 vs 19.02, SSIM 0.5998 vs 0.5781, LPIPS 0.3379 vs 0.3619), and detection without confidence is worse than pixel-aligned baselines, raising robustness questions.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely useful idea for feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting: detecting Gaussian primitives at sub-pixel 2D locations via heatmap/soft-argmax rather than placing one primitive per pixel or per voxel. This directly addresses a real limitation of existing feed-forward 3DGS methods.

The adaptive density mechanism based on per-patch Shannon entropy and the confidence-based multi-view pruning are sensible additions that reduce redundancy. Ablations in Table 4 show that both mechanisms contribute to final performance, especially in LPIPS.

Strong empirical results are reported across six datasets (7Scenes, Charge, DL3DV, SCRREAM, Tanks and Temples, MipNeRF360). The method outperforms AnySplat and DA3-Giant on PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS while using far fewer primitives (e.g., 0.1431 Gaussians/pixel vs. 1.0 for pixel-aligned methods, i.e., roughly 7x fewer).

The paper provides useful geometry evaluation (Table 2) showing that fine-tuning VGGT with the proposed rendering-based losses improves depth and camera pose estimation relative to the original VGGT, while AnySplat degrades it. This supports the claim that the method improves the underlying geometry, not just the rendering decoder.

Qualitative results (Figures 6–9) convincingly show cleaner geometry, fewer floating artifacts, and better extrapolated views than AnySplat and DA3-Giant. Figure 5 also gives a nice visualization of multi-view-aware confidence prediction.

The method is pose-free and trained end-to-end from images without 3D annotations, using photometric and geometry consistency losses. This makes it practically relevant for unposed image collections and aligns with a current research direction.
The paper is generally clear, well illustrated, and the supplementary material adds useful implementation and depth-evaluation details.
weaknesses: The experimental comparison is narrow: only AnySplat and DA3-Giant are used as baselines. Other pose-free or feed-forward 3DGS methods (e.g., NoPoSplat, Splatt3R, PF3Splat, SPFSplat) are discussed but not compared, so the “state-of-the-art” claim is not fully substantiated.

There are technical presentation errors that should be corrected. Equation (1) sums over i,j=0 to P, where P is described as the number of primitives per patch, but the soft-argmax should sum over spatial positions within the heatmap (14x14). The opacity regularization loss L_op = sum sin(alpha(i) * c(i)) does not match the stated goal of pushing opacities to either 0 or 1; a term such as sin(pi * alpha * c) or alpha*c*(1-alpha*c) would be consistent. As written, sin(alpha*c) does not penalize alpha*c=1.

The adaptive density percentages are inconsistent: 55% + 35% + 15% = 105%. This is likely a typo, but it affects reproducibility of the density assignment. The entropy-based density heuristic is also not ablated against random or fixed allocation beyond the 32-Gaussian baseline.

Computational efficiency claims are not fully supported. While the method uses fewer primitives, inference/training runtime and memory are not reported. The backbone is VGGT-1B and the decoder adds a U-Net; without timing, it is unclear whether the method is actually faster than baselines at test time.

The method depends heavily on VGGT pretrained geometry, and the teacher geometry losses keep the model close to VGGT. This reduces the risk of divergence but also limits the demonstrated independence of the approach; it is unclear how well it would work with a weaker or different 3D foundation backbone.

Some evaluation details are not fully specified, such as the exact train/validation splits for the 10 training datasets, loss weights, and the precise test-time alignment protocol. Reproducibility would be stronger with code release or more detailed supplementary description.

The entropy measure is computed on grayscale intensities, which may not always correlate with the number of primitives needed (e.g., smooth but high-frequency edges vs. noisy textures). The paper shows benefit empirically but does not deeply analyze when this heuristic fails.

strengths: **Well-motivated and original core idea.** Reframing feed-forward Gaussian placement as a keypoint-detection problem (DSNT-style heatmaps producing continuous sub-pixel 2D centers, Eq. 1) is a clean conceptual departure from the pixel-aligned and voxel-aligned grid paradigms that dominate prior work (PixelSplat, SplatterImage, AnySplat, MVSplat). The Figure 1 teaser makes the distinction immediately legible, and the analogy to SuperPoint/DSNT is apt rather than superficial.

**Adaptive density allocation is principled and ablated.** Tying per-patch primitive budget to Shannon entropy of local grayscale histograms (following APT) is a sensible, non-arbitrary criterion, and Table 4 confirms it matters (19.09 vs. 17.80 PSNR, 0.3379 vs. 0.4459 LPIPS). Figure 4's visualization of the low/medium/high density heatmap channels is genuine, informative evidence that the model specializes channels for borders/corners.

**Consistent empirical gains with substantially fewer primitives.** Table 1 shows the method outperforming AnySplat and DA3-Giant across six datasets and four view counts (3/6/9/12) at 0.141 #G/pix versus 0.841 and 1.0. The compression claim is not just a metric artifact: Figure 6 and Figure 7 qualitatively show reduced floaters, sharper geometry, and no visible voxel grid under extrapolation, which is exactly the failure mode the paper targets.

**Careful, honest experimental hygiene.** Test-time alignment is performed without test-time optimization of camera parameters, the alignment protocol is described explicitly (single scale factor from context poses), and the Limitations section candidly enumerates missing visible regions, no view-dependent color, and failure on human subjects. Table 2's geometry evaluation (where DA3-Giant is better on depth and camera pose, and the proposed method only wins on intrinsics) is reported as-is rather than cherry-picked.

**Multi-view confidence pruning is a genuinely useful mechanism.** Figure 5 is a compelling qualitative demonstration that the model learns view-dependent redundancy (Gaussians from image 4 discarded once image 6 observes the face), and the confidence map is learned implicitly from the self-rendering/full-model dual rendering scheme rather than supervised. This is a nice design.

**Adequate reproducibility.** The supplementary material specifies the VGGT-1B checkpoint, Pytorch-UNet implementation, 13 input channels, 32 output channels, softmax temperature 0.2, grid_sample padding mode, and depth-head behavior. Teacher-geometry and opacity regularization losses are given with formulas. This is well above average detail for a CVPR submission.
weaknesses: **Evaluation breadth is narrow for a 'state-of-the-art' claim.** Quantitative comparison is restricted to AnySplat and DA3-Giant. Other feed-forward 3DGS methods operating under comparable pose-free or few-view settings (PF3Splat, SPFSplat, NoPoSplat, Splat3R, Splatter Image, Flash3D) are discussed in Related Work but never benchmarked. The Section 4.1 claim that the method 'significantly outperforms AnySplat and DepthAnything3' is supported, but 'state-of-the-art for feed-forward models' (Abstract, Conclusion) is not established by two baselines.

**Potential training/evaluation dataset overlap needs clarification.** The training set is described as 'subsets of 10 datasets: DL3DV [31], Co3Dv2, WildRGBD, BlendedMVS, UnrealStereo4K, RealEstate10k, ARKitScenes, DTU, ScanNet++ and KITTI360,' while DL3DV is also an evaluation dataset ('DL3DV benchmark [31] contains 140 indoor and outdoor scenes'). The 140-scene DL3DV-10K test split is presumably disjoint from training, but the paper never states the split explicitly. This should be resolved; if there is any overlap, the headline Table 1 numbers are compromised.

**Ablation does not isolate several claimed contributions.** Table 4 ablates only adaptive density and confidence pruning. There is no ablation for the geometry consistency losses (L_depth, L_normal), the teacher geometry losses (L_teacher_D, L_teacher_t, L_teacher_R), or the opacity regularization — all of which are presented as necessary for stability ('fine-tuning solely with photometric loss is not stable and causes the model to diverge'). The opacity regularizer in particular is credited with fixing the half-transparency problem in Figure 7, but its effect is never measured. The loss stack is heavy and its individual value is unverified.

**The headline efficiency metric is partly definitional.** The '#G/pix' ratio compares against pixel-aligned methods that are constrained by construction to exactly one primitive per input pixel. Reporting a 7x reduction over a baseline whose ratio is fixed at 1.0 is somewhat self-fulfilling. A more informative efficiency analysis would report quality at matched primitive counts (e.g., a PSNR-vs-#Gaussian Pareto curve against AnySplat at multiple density settings), which is feasible given the paper's own adaptive density knobs.

**The sub-pixel placement gain is modest and only compared against one offset baseline.** Table 3 shows +0.30 dB PSNR / +0.014 SSIM over pixel-aligned, which is real but small, and the alternative 'off-grid' design space is represented only by SplatterImage's 3D offset. The paper asserts that 'placing primitives accurately requires more advanced techniques' but does not test intermediate designs (e.g., offsets with the same adaptive density, or learned 2D offsets without heatmap detection), so it is unclear how much of the benefit comes from the detection formulation versus simply from breaking the grid.

**Test-time alignment still uses ground-truth reference poses.** The evaluation protocol aligns predicted cameras to GT via Umeyama with a scale factor, and the reported numbers depend on this alignment. While this follows AnySplat's protocol and no optimization is performed, pose-free evaluation under GT-pose alignment can obscure pose errors; the claimed camera-pose quality is only assessed indirectly through Table 2. A no-alignment or relative-pose metric would strengthen the pose-free claim.

**Minor: some claims outrun the evidence.** The conclusion asserts the decoder 'should open the possibility to process 3DGS models from high resolution images' without any high-resolution experiment, and the abstract's 'outperforms competitors' is broader than the two-method comparison supports. The hard-coded pruning threshold αc < 0.1 and the entropy percentile splits (55%/35%/15%) are also introduced without sensitivity analysis.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and technically sensible: adapting DSNT/soft-argmax keypoint detection to predict sub-pixel 2D Gaussian centers, thereby escaping the rigid pixel/voxel grid. This is a meaningful conceptual departure from the dominant pixel-aligned and voxel-aligned paradigms.

The paper combines several complementary mechanisms (off-grid detection, entropy-based adaptive density, confidence-based multi-view pruning) and validates them with ablations. Table 4 shows a clear gain from adaptive density + confidence (PSNR 17.80 → 19.09; LPIPS 0.4459 → 0.3379), and Table 3 isolates the placement contribution.

Empirical coverage is reasonably broad: six datasets (DL3DV, Charge, SCRREAM, 7scenes, Tanks and Temples, MipNeRF360) with 3/6/9/12 views, and consistent improvements over AnySplat and DA3-Giant (Table 1, average PSNR 21.21 vs. 17.71/18.83) at a much lower primitive count (#G/pix 0.141, ~7x fewer than pixel-aligned).

The observation that fine-tuning the VGGT backbone under photometric supervision improves depth and camera/intrinsics estimation (Table 2) is a useful secondary finding, and the geometry loss design (depth, normal, teacher-geometry regularization) is described with enough detail to be implementable.

The limitations section is candid about holes, view-dependent effects, and lack of human representation, and the supplementary gives concrete implementation details (channel counts, softmax temperature, grid_sample padding, loss weights), which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The paper's headline contribution (off-grid primitive placement) has only a modest measured effect. In the controlled ablation of Table 3, replacing pixel-aligned placement with the proposed off-grid detection changes PSNR from 19.01 to 19.22 (+0.21 dB) on Tanks and Temples/MipNeRF360. The large gains over AnySplat therefore appear to come mostly from other factors (fine-tuning, confidence pruning, geometry losses), so the central narrative overstates the role of off-grid detection relative to the evidence.

The state-of-the-art claim is only supported against two feed-forward baselines (AnySplat and DepthAnything3-Giant). Other directly relevant pose-free/feed-forward 3DGS methods (e.g., NoPoSplat, Splatt3R, PF3Splat, MVSplat, PixelSplat, FreeSplat) are discussed in related work but never compared quantitatively, so 'state-of-the-art' is not adequately established.

The technical novelty is largely a recombination of existing ideas: soft-argmax/DSNT for sub-pixel localization, entropy-based density allocation (explicitly borrowed from APT), and confidence-based multi-view pruning/aggregation (already used, e.g., by AnySplat's voxel aggregation). The paper does not clearly articulate what is fundamentally new beyond the application of these components to Gaussian placement.

Efficiency claims are not substantiated with runtime or memory measurements. The abstract/introduction assert scene generation 'in seconds,' yet no inference-time or memory comparison is provided, and training requires 140 GB VRAM, which raises practical reproducibility concerns.

There are apparent inconsistencies in the reported numbers for the same datasets across tables (e.g., Tanks and Temples: PSNR 18.37/SSIM 0.5982 in Table 1 vs. 19.22/0.6064 in Table 3; MipNeRF360: 18.36 in Table 1 vs. 18.03 in Table 3). These are not explained (different view counts? subsets?), which undermines confidence in the evaluation protocol.

The reliance on a large pretrained backbone (VGGT-1B) and its teacher-geometry regularization means the reported gains conflate the proposed decoder with improvements to the underlying geometry model, making it harder to attribute the improvement to the paper's actual contributions.
